items.title: Agent Experience: The Third Reader of Everything You Build
items.label: Small Web
items.excerpt:
Watch a coding agent work for ten minutes in a repository it has never seen, and count the guesses: which command runs the tests, whether the linter’s complaint is fatal, what the deployment tool means by two paragraphs of prose and a stack trace, which of the three services called billing the ticket is about, and whether the README is still true. Each guess costs tokens and time, some are wrong, and the wrong ones end up in a pull request.

Hardly any of those guesses say something about the model. They come from the system the agent was dropped into, and most of them can be designed away. How well a system serves the agents that now do much of its work has become a design concern of its own, and this post is my attempt to describe it.

The developer moved up a level

In Almost Irrelevant I argued that once agents write most of the code, the choice of programming language matters much less than it did, because the agent absorbs the learning curve, the ceremony and the boilerplate…

items.title: Monday Morning Greetings 2026 #47 – The Good Old Days, or Were They?
items.label: Blogs
items.excerpt:
🫧 Open on Bubbles

You be the judge. It was 1976 in Vrindavan, the year I came.

 

I arrived in May, and it was brutally hot. When there was electricity, I slept under a fan. I kept a bucket of water beside my bed and would dip my gamcha in it and spread it over me, but whoosh! In half a second, it was bone dry.

 

And about that electricity. There was a single transformer for all of Raman Reti, so there was load-shedding. To keep the system from being drained, the power was cut for hours every day, usually at the critical moment when everyone needed it most.

 

The building was concrete, so it held the heat. It was a “concrete heater” until the rainy season cooled it, and until then there was little relief.

 

When the rains finally came, there was some relief. Or was there? The wells weren’t deep enough, so during the monsoon, the rising water table threatened to be contaminated with whatever seeped into the ground. Water also pooled, stagnated, and turned swampy once the earth…

items.title: Feed the Scorchpot [$14.99] [Strategy] [Windows] [macOS]
items.label: Gaming
items.excerpt:
You struck a deal with a dragon: twenty years of protection for twenty years of dinner service. The island thrives under the beast's watchful eye, as long as the meals keep coming.

Every year, the dragon wakes up hungrier. You roll dice to work your island, harvest ingredients, fuse them into recipes, and cook them down in the Scorchpot — the pot you keep full or end up in. Get the meal right and you prosper. Get it wrong and you're smoke.

Build farmsteads, shrines, and harbors across your hex-grid island, each one changing how the board pays out. The best runs start with a handful of tiles and end with a machine that buries the dragon in food. Then the odds tighten, the dragon turns picky, and you tear the whole thing down and rebuild while it's on fire.

Feed the Scorchpot, keep the dragon happy, and outlast the contract.
